SIMP

symplectic integrators for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

SIMP (Symplectic Integrators for Monte-Carlo Proposals) integrates Hamiltonian systems and builds the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo proposals that run on them.

The integrators are splitting schemes: an alternating sequence of position and momentum updates whose coefficients define the method. A symplectic scheme conserves a nearby energy, so a trajectory keeps its total energy within a bounded band over long horizons and the proposals it produces are accepted at high rates. Leapfrog and the Yoshida order 4, 6 and 8 members come from a single triple-jump composition, so the whole family shares one stepper and one coefficient source, written as header-only C++. You can compare schemes on your target by their energy error and their gradient cost per step, and choose the one that drives your sampler.

SIMP supports:

  • A family of schemes. Leapfrog, the two-stage minimum-error member minerror2 and Yoshida orders 4, 6 and 8. simp_schemes() lists each with its order and gradient evaluations per step.
  • Coefficients tuned to the step band. The "adaptive2" and "adaptive3" schemes take the two- or three-stage weights that minimise the worst-case energy error on a Gaussian target over a band of dimensionless steps, computed from an exact harmonic analysis. simp_b_optimal() returns the weights for a given band.
  • Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. simp_hmc() draws each proposal by integrating the target’s Hamiltonian flow and accepts it by the Metropolis rule on the energy, with any scheme as the integrator.
  • Split potentials. simp_integrate_mts() advances a potential split into a slow and a fast part at two rates (RESPA), so the fast part takes small inner steps without evaluating the slow part at the same rate.
  • Non-separable Hamiltonians. simp_integrate_nonsep() uses the generalized (implicit) leapfrog, as in Riemannian dynamics with a position-dependent mass.
  • A C++ core for other packages. The steppers are scalar-templated headers in inst/include. A package reaches them with LinkingTo: SIMP and drives them with its own gradient, under automatic differentiation as well as in double precision.

Installation

SIMP compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools matching your R version
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install SIMP from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/SIMP")

The C++ code uses the Eigen headers that RcppEigen supplies and needs no system library.

Usage

  1. Write the gradient of the potential energy U(q) as an R function of the position.
  2. Call simp_integrate() with a starting position and momentum, the gradient, the step size and the number of steps.
  3. Sample a target with simp_hmc(), which runs the same integrator inside each proposal.

The potential of a unit Gaussian target is U(q) = 0.5 q'q, so its gradient is q. Starting on the unit circle in phase space, the exact flow is a rotation:

library(SIMP)

grad_U <- function(q) q
out <- simp_integrate(q0 = c(1, 0), p0 = c(0, 1), grad_U = grad_U,
                      eps = 0.1, n_steps = 60)
out$q
#> [1]  0.9608666 -0.2773584

The result is a list with the endpoint position q and momentum p. The default integrator is leapfrog, and integrator takes any name that simp_schemes() lists:

simp_schemes()
#>   integrator order gradient_evals
#> 1   leapfrog     2              1
#> 2  minerror2     2              2
#> 3   yoshida4     4              3
#> 4   yoshida6     6              9
#> 5   yoshida8     8             27

trajectory = TRUE returns every step, and a potential U passed to the call records the total energy along it.

Sampling with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

simp_hmc() takes the potential and its gradient. For a bivariate Gaussian with correlation 0.8, the potential uses the precision matrix:

Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2)
P <- chol2inv(chol(Sigma))
U <- function(q) 0.5 * as.numeric(t(q) %*% P %*% q)
grad_U <- function(q) as.numeric(P %*% q)

fit <- simp_hmc(U, grad_U, init = c(0, 0), n_iter = 2000, eps = 0.25,
                n_steps = 16, warmup = 500, integrator = "minerror2")
colMeans(fit$draws)
#> [1] -0.0005825939 -0.0005670790
fit$accept_rate
#> [1] 1

The sample means are close to the target mean of zero. Symplectic integration with SIMP compares the energy error of leapfrog, minerror2 and yoshida4 at the same step size on this kind of target.

Non-separable and split Hamiltonians

When the kinetic and potential parts do not separate, as with a position-dependent mass, simp_integrate_nonsep() solves the two implicit stages of the generalized leapfrog by fixed-point iteration. For a separable Hamiltonian it reduces to the standard leapfrog. simp_integrate_mts() handles a potential split into a stiff, cheap part and a smooth, expensive part, with m inner substeps of the fast part per outer step. Symplectic integration with SIMP runs the generalized leapfrog on a mass of 1 + 0.5 q^2.

Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the GitHub issues. A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with reprex.
